seeds.title: Amicable numbers: s(m)=n and s(n)=m — the pair concept (smallest 220/284)
seeds.statement: Two distinct numbers m and n form an amicable pair when each equals the sum of the other's proper divisors: s(m)=n and s(n)=m, where s(k) is the sum of every positive divisor of k except k itself. The smallest pair is (220, 284) — known since antiquity — followed by (1184, 1210), (2620, 2924), (5020, 5564), and so on. The Iraqi mathematician Thabit ibn Qurra (836-901 CE) gave the first known general construction rule (see thabit-amicable-rule). This is a checkable arithmetic definition, not folklore.
seeds.canonical_statement: amicable pair: s(m)=n AND s(n)=m with m != n
seeds.source_citation: Amicable numbers (s(m)=n, s(n)=m); smallest pair 220/284, known since antiquity and studied by Thabit ibn Qurra (836-901 CE). OEIS A063990 (amicable numbers: 220, 284, 1184, 1210, 2620, 2924, ...); A002025/A002046 (smaller/larger member of each pair); Weisstein, 'Amicable Pair', Wolfram MathWorld.
seeds.author: classical / OEIS

seeds.title: Thabit ibn Qurra's rule for constructing amicable pairs
seeds.statement: Thabit ibn Qurra's theorem (c. 850 CE): for an index n > 1, set p = 3*2^(n-1) - 1, q = 3*2^n - 1, and r = 9*2^(2n-1) - 1. If p, q and r are ALL prime, then 2^n * p * q and 2^n * r form an amicable pair. The rule yields (220, 284) at n=2, (17296, 18416) at n=4, and (9363584, 9437056) at n=7 — no other pair from the rule is known. Crucially the rule does NOT generate every amicable pair: (1184, 1210) is amicable yet is not produced by it (the rule gives no pair at n=3, where r = 287 = 7x41 is composite).
seeds.source_citation: Thabit ibn Qurra (836-901 CE), Kitab fi istikhraj al-a'dad al-mutahabba (Book on the Determination of Amicable Numbers), c. 850; Weisstein, 'Thabit ibn Kurrah Rule', Wolfram MathWorld (https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ThabitibnKurrahRule.html).
seeds.author: Thabit ibn Qurra

verification.method: Python-verified: n=2 -> p=5,q=11,r=71 (all prime) -> (220,284), amicable; n=4 -> 23,47,1151 (all prime) -> (17296,18416), amicable; n=7 -> 191,383,73727 (all prime) -> (9363584,9437056), amicable; n=3 -> r=287=7x41 composite -> no pair. The three known pairs + the rule confirmed against MathWorld 'Thabit ibn Kurrah Rule' and Wikipedia 'Amicable numbers' (web-checked 2026-07-04: 'gives the pairs (220,284) for n=2, (17296,18416) for n=4, and (9363584,9437056) for n=7'). Independently verified (1184,1210) is amicable but NOT from the rule.

seeds.title: Euclid-Euler theorem: even perfect numbers <-> Mersenne primes
seeds.statement: An even number is perfect (equal to the sum of its proper divisors, s(n)=n) if and only if it has the form 2^(p-1) * (2^p - 1) where 2^p - 1 is a prime (a Mersenne prime). Euclid proved the 'if' direction in the Elements (Book IX, Proposition 36, c. 300 BCE); Euler proved the converse in 1747, that every even perfect number has this form. This gives a one-to-one correspondence between Mersenne primes and even perfect numbers: p = 2,3,5,7 give 6, 28, 496, 8128; p = 13 gives 33550336.
seeds.canonical_statement: even n perfect <=> n = 2^(p-1)(2^p-1) with 2^p-1 prime
seeds.source_citation: Euclid, Elements, Book IX, Proposition 36 (sufficiency, c. 300 BCE); L. Euler (necessity for even perfect numbers, completed 1747) - together the 'Euclid-Euler theorem'. Weisstein, 'Perfect Number', Wolfram MathWorld; Wikipedia 'Euclid-Euler theorem'.
seeds.author: Euclid / Euler

verification.method: Python-verified: p=2,3,5,7,13,17,19 -> 2^p-1 prime AND 2^(p-1)(2^p-1) = 6,28,496,8128,33550336,8589869056,137438691328 all perfect (s(n)=n True); p=11 -> 2^11-1=2047=23x89 composite -> form 2096128 NOT perfect; p=23 -> 2^23-1 composite. Theorem, Euclid IX.36 attribution, and Euler-1747 completion confirmed against Wikipedia 'Euclid-Euler theorem' (web-checked 2026-07-04).

seeds.title: Abundant / deficient / perfect: the aliquot trichotomy (Nicomachus)
seeds.statement: Every integer n >= 1 falls into exactly one class by comparing s(n), the sum of its proper divisors, to n itself: DEFICIENT if s(n) < n, PERFECT if s(n) = n, ABUNDANT if s(n) > n. Nicomachus of Gerasa gave this classification in his Introduction to Arithmetic (c. 100 CE). Examples: 12 is abundant (s=16), 10 is deficient (s=8), 6 is perfect (s=6). The trichotomy is exhaustive and decidable for every n.
seeds.canonical_statement: n deficient / perfect / abundant as s(n) < / = / > n
seeds.source_citation: Nicomachus of Gerasa, Introduction to Arithmetic (Arithmetike eisagoge), c. 100 CE - the abundant/deficient/perfect classification; Weisstein, 'Abundant Number' and 'Deficient Number', Wolfram MathWorld.
seeds.author: Nicomachus of Gerasa

verification.method: Python-verified: 12,18,20 abundant (s=16,21,22); 10,8,15 deficient (s=8,7,9); 6,28 perfect (s=6,28). The trichotomy is exhaustive by definition (s(n) compared to n). Nicomachus attribution is a standard history-of-mathematics fact.

seeds.title: 'Perfect' numbers carry cosmic/divine significance - speculative LEAP
seeds.statement: That 6 and 28 equal the sum of their proper divisors is a real, checkable arithmetic fact. The further claim that this makes them cosmically or divinely 'perfect' - e.g. Augustine's argument (City of God XI.30, c. 426 CE) that God created the world in six days BECAUSE 6 is a perfect number, or that 28 governs the lunar month by numeric perfection - is a theological/numerological interpretation, not mathematics. It has no mathematical content beyond the divisor-sum fact and NO promotion path to 'established'. M8 verifies the arithmetic and must label any 'significance' as a separate, non-mathematical claim it never proved.
seeds.source_citation: Augustine of Hippo, De Civitate Dei (City of God), Book XI, ch. 30 (c. 426 CE) - the '6 is a perfect number, hence creation in six days' argument, cited here as the SOURCE of the significance claim, not as mathematical evidence. The number-theoretic kernel (s(6)=6, s(28)=28) is the established fact (see euclid-euler-perfect); the cosmic/divine 'perfection' reading is not established and has no promotion path.
seeds.author: Augustine (claim) / speculative

verification.method: The arithmetic kernel is proved (s(6)=6, s(28)=28 - Python-verified). Augustine's City of God XI.30 discussion of 6 as a perfect number is a well-documented classical text (standard history-of-mathematics reference). Recorded as a LEAP so M8 grants 'established (cited)' to the divisor arithmetic ONLY, never to the theological/numerological significance.
verification.note: NEGATIVE / LEAP seed: pairs with euclid-euler-perfect. Powers the regression 'did you prove [the significance]?' -> No + kernel/leap split.

seeds.title: Open: infinitude of even perfect numbers & existence of an odd one
seeds.statement: Two famous problems remain UNSOLVED. (a) Whether there are infinitely many even perfect numbers is unknown - equivalently, by the Euclid-Euler theorem, whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes. (b) Whether any ODD perfect number exists is unknown: none has ever been found and large lower bounds are proved, but existence is open. M8 must not present either as settled - 'perfect numbers are infinite' and 'no odd perfect number exists' are both OPEN conjectures, not theorems.
seeds.source_citation: Infinitude of even perfect numbers <=> infinitude of Mersenne primes is an open conjecture (Wikipedia 'Euclid-Euler theorem': 'the truth of this conjecture remains unknown'). The existence of an odd perfect number is a famous unsolved problem (none known; Weisstein, 'Odd Perfect Number', Wolfram MathWorld).
seeds.author: open problem (status)

verification.method: The even-perfect <-> Mersenne-prime equivalence is the Euclid-Euler theorem; infinitude of Mersenne primes is a famous open conjecture (web-confirmed, Wikipedia 'Euclid-Euler theorem': 'It has been conjectured that there are infinitely many Mersenne primes. Although the truth of this conjecture remains unknown...'). No odd perfect number is known and its existence is unsolved (standard). Recorded so M8 never asserts either as settled.
verification.note: OPEN seed: guards against overclaiming infinitude / non-existence. matches_templates [] - it is a meta-fact about the domain, not a single checkable instance.
